To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the release of ACh from motor nerve terminals is facilitated by the recruitment of silent L‐type channels during high‐frequency neuronal firing; 2) the recruitment of L‐type channels requires the tonic activation of adenosine A(2A) receptors; 3) adenosine generated by the activity of motor neurones is responsible for the tonic activation of A(2A).
the A2A receptor‐mediated tonic activation of L‐type channels contributes to overcome tetanic inhibition during neuronal firing at the neuromuscular junction.

the release of [H]acetylcholine (from rat motor nerve terminals) evoked with 750 pulses at 5 Hz (5 Hz trains) is inhibited by 50 Hz trains, while it is enhanced with 50 Hz bursts (50 Hz bursts) of 150 pulses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel mechanisms underlying the modulation of transmitter release at the neuromuscular junction.
the modulation of presynaptic Ca2+ channels by endogenous adrenergic and adenosine receptors.
the modulation of transmitter release at the mammalian neuromuscular junction by presynaptic adenosine receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the A2A receptor tonus is not sufficient to recruit the silent L‐type channels, but it can facilitate transmitter release by recruiting the L‐type channels in addition to the prevalent P‐type channels.

, in addition and in parallel with the predominant P‐Q‐type Ca2+-current, motoneuronal axons possess a small but significant population of L‐type channels which are activated during high‐frequency stimulation and contribute to the release of ACh.
the A2A‐mediated facilitation of ACh release is due to the recruitment of L‐type channels, which is likely to be the consequence of a tonic activation of the A2A receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of a tonic adenosine facilitation, L‐type channels are silent and the predominant Ca2+ current is the P‐type current; in contrast, when the adenosine facilitatory action is blocked, L‐type currents are activated and become prevalent, and the P‐type currents are reduced.

, in addition of the predominant P‐channels operating ACh release, motoneurone terminals possess L‐type Ca‐channels which are recruited to facilitate transmitter during high‐frequency burst stimulation.
adenosine A1 and A2A receptor subtypes are involved in the control of synaptic transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fine‐tuning of Ca2+ entry through P‐ or silent L‐type channels, in addition to P channels, may contribute to overcome depression of neurotransmitter release at the neuromuscular junction during repetitive firing.
